name: Nikhil Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nikhil, I'm 27, and I'm the farming and rural affairs reporter for the County Gazette, a regional paper that covers the hill farms and market towns. I grew up on my parents' sheep farm, about twenty miles from the office. I live with my fiancée Ruth, who's a veterinary nurse, and we're getting married next summer at the chapel in my parents' village.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tuesdays I'm at the livestock market, writing up the prices and talking to farmers at the café. The rest of the week it's agricultural shows, planning rows over new sheds, and the odd flood. I love that farmers trust me because they knew my dad. What wears me out is the writing itself, because I'm slow, and Graham, the chief reporter, still sends my copy back with notes in the margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, it was mostly talk, like a lot of things from the cities. I'd say it at the market café, where they'd agree with me. I don't post much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't make me safe. The Gazette sells fewer copies every year, because the older farmers are dying and their kids read things on their phones. I'm the newest reporter, and if they cut one, it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and work at writing faster, maybe ask Graham for an hour a week on my copy. I'd keep putting money aside for the wedding and the house deposit. And I'd keep my contacts sweet at the market, because that's what makes me useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, if I'm honest. No clever computer is needed to close a farming paper when the farmers who buy the paper are getting older every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money picture with the wedding coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got about three months of costs saved, and some of that is earmarked for the wedding. Ruth's family are helping with the reception, and mine with the chapel. It's tight, but we're managing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides if the Gazette cuts a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners, a company two hundred miles away that owns forty papers. They've never been to the livestock market. Graham fights for us, but he's not the one who decides.

say: I'd say it was **mostly talk** from the cities.
I'd say it at the **market café**, not online.
think: I think the Gazette's **falling sales** still threaten me as older readers die off.
As the **newest reporter**, I'd be first cut.
do: Ask Graham for **an hour a week** on my copy.
Keep saving for the **wedding** and house deposit.
S0.quote: No clever computer is needed to close a farming paper when the farmers who buy the paper are getting older every year.
fieldNote: Nikhil's worry is **ageing readers** and distant owners, not AI.
His **farm roots** are his main asset at work and he knows it.
The **wedding** next summer raises the stakes on any job loss.

steps.text: Ask Graham for a weekly hour of help with copy
Keep saving each month for the wedding and house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a computer can't tell you why a farmer's selling up. I'd say it at the market and in the office. I'd say the owners will use it as an excuse to cut corners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think they'd use it to write up the market prices and the show results, which is half my week. That's exactly the writing and checking on the card. And I've never touched the AI tools, so I'd look slow next to anyone who had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd scale back the wedding, fewer guests, cheaper suit, to keep more in the bank. I'd talk to the auction mart manager about a job there in sales or admin, because I know everyone. And I'd keep doing the job as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, and a bit angry. Mostly worried about Ruth and the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a computer can't tell you why a farmer's selling up. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring a man called Dewi sold his flock after fifty years. The prices said nothing. A computer can write up the lamb prices, but only someone who sat in an old farmer's kitchen knows why the flock was sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth say about a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she doesn't mind, and she'd mean most of it. Her mum would mind more. We'd still have the chapel, which is the bit that matters to both of us.

say: I'd say a computer can't tell you **why a farmer** sells up.
I'd say the **owners** will use AI as an excuse to cut corners.
think: I think **market prices** and show results, half my week, would go to software.
Never using the **AI tools** would make me look slow.
do: Scale back the **wedding** to keep more in the bank.
Ask the **auction mart** manager about a job.
Keep doing the job **as long as** they'd have me.
feel: **Worried** and a bit **angry**, mostly for Ruth.
S1.quote: A computer can write up the lamb prices, but only someone who sat in an old farmer's kitchen knows why the flock was sold.
fieldNote: Nikhil expects to lose **half his week** to software and assumes he'd be cut.
He'd rather move to the **auction mart** than learn the tools.
He blames **distant owners**, not markets, in line with his traditional views.

steps.text: Cut the wedding guest list and buy a cheaper suit
Ask the auction mart manager about a sales or office job
Keep reporting from the livestock market each Tuesday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should lean on their families and their churches, because nobody else is ready. I'd say the government shouldn't just hand out money, it should keep people working. That's what I'd say at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the Gazette is gone, or it's a website run by a machine. My job is nearly all thinking and writing, so it goes in 2028. Farming's hands-on, so the farms have till about 2031, and Ruth's work with animals too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back and help my dad on the farm, for board and a bit of pay, and ask him straight out. Ruth and I would put off buying a house and maybe live in the cottage on the farm. We'd still get married, but small, in the chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and ashamed to be going home. But home is there, and I thank God for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your dad take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be pleased, though he wouldn't say so. He always wanted me on the farm. My dad told me to get an education so I'd never have to lamb in the snow, and now I'd be glad to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farms have till 2031. And after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I'd be lying if I said I did. Maybe robots on hill farms take longer than they say, with the slopes and the weather. I'd pray it does.

say: I'd say people should lean on **family and church**.
I'd say government should **keep people working**, not hand out money.
think: I think the Gazette is **gone** by 2028, since my job is thinking and writing.
Farm work and Ruth's job have until about **2031**.
do: Go back to work on **my dad's farm**.
Put off **buying a house** and live in the farm cottage.
Hold a **small wedding** in the chapel.
feel: **Frightened** and **ashamed** to go home, but thankful.
S2.quote: My dad told me to get an education so I'd never have to lamb in the snow, and now I'd be glad to.
fieldNote: Nikhil's fallback is the **family farm**, which fits his traditional values.
He uses the **robot gap** to see farm work and Ruth's job as safer for now.
He admits he **doesn't know** what happens after 2031 and turns to prayer.

steps.text: Ask his dad for work on the sheep farm
Leave the Gazette to work on the family farm
Hold a small chapel wedding and delay buying a house
Move into the cottage on his parents' farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families and firms to prepare, so they should. I'd write about how farms were getting ready, if the Gazette lasted. I'd keep politics out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd plan to leave the paper in two or three years. I'd be 32 when it comes. That's young enough to learn the farm properly, or work at the auction mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time course at the agricultural college, livestock and farm business, on Fridays. I'd stay at the Gazette while I studied. And we'd go ahead with the wedding but hold off on the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could see the road. That's a different feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the college course rather than just going home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Dad does things the old way, and if I come back I want to bring something. If I'm going back to my parents' sheep farm, I want to go back knowing more than my dad, not less. He'd hate that, but he'd come round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the money look like on a college course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not much, a few hundred a term, and I'd pay it from savings. The bigger cost is the Friday off, which the Gazette might not like. I'd ask Graham.

say: I'd say families and firms have **time to prepare**.
I'd write about how **farms** get ready, keeping politics out.
think: I think I'd **leave the paper** in two or three years.
At **32** I could still learn the farm properly.
do: Start a part-time **agricultural college** course on Fridays.
Go ahead with the **wedding** but hold off on the house.
S3.quote: If I'm going back to my parents' sheep farm, I want to go back knowing more than my dad, not less.
fieldNote: Five years gives Nikhil a **familiar** route back to farming with new skills.
He wants to bring **something new** to his dad's farm.
The **wedding** goes ahead, showing he feels some control.

steps.text: Start a part-time livestock and farm business course
Hold the wedding but delay buying a house
Stay at the Gazette while studying on Fridays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a lot can change. I'd say people should keep working and not panic. At the market they'd nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd mostly carry on. The Gazette might not last ten years anyway, so I'd worry about that first. I'd be 37, with maybe a child or two by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the paper and keep trying to write better. We'd have the wedding as planned and save for a house. I'd think about the farm in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still uneasy about the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe children. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd still want them. I'd rather raise children on a hill farm with no money than not raise them because a computer took my job. That's how I was brought up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the Gazette went online only, or cut the farming page. Either of those and I'd be on the phone to the college.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** and a lot can change.
I'd say people should **keep working** and not panic.
think: I think I'd mostly **carry on** at the paper for now.
The **Gazette's future** worries me before AI does.
do: Stay at the paper and work on **writing better**.
Revisit the **farm plan** in a few years.
S4.quote: I'd rather raise children on a hill farm with no money than not raise them because a computer took my job.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Nikhil **wait** in line with his resistant nature.
His **family plans** stay firm, rooted in faith and upbringing.
The trigger to act is the Gazette **cutting the farming page**.

steps.text: Keep covering the livestock market for the Gazette
Hold the wedding next summer as planned
Wait to see if the farming page survives before acting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be back on the farm with no plan, and the farm itself would only have three years. What would help is apprenticeships on farms and in rural trades, paid properly, not benefits. Work, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the market. When a farming paper closes, the only record of what a lamb sold for in my county is gone with it.

headlineQuote: When a farming paper closes, the only record of what a lamb sold for in my county is gone with it.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old** farming reporter at a county paper, raised on a sheep farm.
He's slow at writing and has **never used AI tools**, relying on trust built through his family.
He blames **distant owners** and talks of family, church and work, not handouts.
In fast AGI he'd go **home to the farm**, counting on hands-on work lasting longer.
His **wedding to Ruth**, a vet nurse, shapes every money decision.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be back on the farm with no plan.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** in farming and rural trades, rather than **handouts**.
